subtopic_detail: Sticky eyes with lid swelling first appearing on day ten of life in a baby born vaginally at term
stem:
A 10 day old baby girl is brought to your general practice because both her eyes have been gluey since yesterday and her lids look puffy. She was born at term by normal vaginal birth after an uncomplicated pregnancy, and her mother had no antenatal screening swabs taken.

She is feeding well and gaining weight. Her mother mentions that she has been a little snuffly but has no cough. On examination the conjunctivae are injected with a copious sticky discharge and moderate lid oedema, and the corneas are clear on fluorescein staining. You take a swab for nucleic acid testing before starting treatment.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 138/min, blood pressure 72/44 mmHg, respiratory rate 44/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Bilateral conjunctival injection with copious sticky discharge, moderate lid oedema, clear corneas on fluorescein staining, red reflex present bilaterally
data_table.Growth: Weight 3.6 kg, tracking along the birth centile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Oral azithromycin for the baby and referral of both parents for testing and treatment
options.rationale: Onset at the end of the first week with copious discharge and lid oedema points to a genitally acquired organism, which needs systemic rather than topical therapy because it also colonises the nasopharynx and can cause pneumonitis. Treating the parents prevents reinfection and addresses their own untreated infection. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Topical chloramphenicol eye drops for the baby with review arranged in forty eight hours
options.rationale: Topical therapy does not clear nasopharyngeal carriage and so does not prevent the later respiratory complication. It would be reasonable for an uncomplicated bacterial conjunctivitis in an older infant. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Saline eye toilet and reassurance, with review only if the discharge has not settled
options.rationale: Saline toilet alone is appropriate for a blocked tear duct, which presents with watering rather than this degree of purulent discharge and lid swelling. Withholding treatment here risks progression. (Source: RCH CPG: Conjunctivitis)

options.text: Admit for intravenous cefotaxime and hourly saline irrigation of both eyes
options.rationale: This intensity of treatment is reserved for the hyperacute presentation of a different genital organism, which characteristically appears in the first days of life with marked chemosis and corneal risk. The timing and corneal findings here do not fit. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Oral aciclovir for the baby with urgent ophthalmology review the same day
options.rationale: Antiviral therapy is directed at a vesicular or dendritic presentation, and the fluorescein stain here shows no dendritic ulcer. Copious purulent discharge is not the expected pattern. (Source: RCH CPG: Conjunctivitis)

explanation.summary: Neonatal conjunctivitis is stratified by the day of onset because that determines the likely organism and therefore the route of treatment. Presentation within the first few days with marked chemosis suggests gonococcal infection and is a sight threatening emergency needing parenteral therapy. Onset towards the end of the first week or in the second week suggests chlamydial infection, which requires oral macrolide therapy because the organism also colonises the nasopharynx and can produce an afebrile pneumonitis at four to twelve weeks. Diagnosis of either in a neonate is also a diagnosis in the parents, so contact testing and treatment are part of the management.
key_points: Day of onset is the primary discriminator in neonatal conjunctivitis
Chlamydial infection needs oral not topical therapy because of nasopharyngeal carriage
Untreated chlamydial carriage can cause an afebrile pneumonitis weeks later
A swab for nucleic acid testing is taken before treatment starts
Parental testing and treatment are part of managing the neonate
explanation.pearls: Chlamydial conjunctivitis typically declares itself between day five and day fourteen, and the oral macrolide is given to prevent the pneumonitis that can follow at four to twelve weeks, not merely to clear the eye.

subtopic_detail: Timing of birth for intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy when the bile acid level exceeds one hundred micromol per litre
stem:
A 31 year old woman at 33 weeks in her first pregnancy attends your antenatal clinic with three weeks of itching, worst on her palms and the soles of her feet and worse at night. She has no rash apart from scratch marks.

Her pregnancy has otherwise been uncomplicated with normal growth on serial scans and normal blood pressure throughout. Her urine shows no protein. A viral hepatitis screen and liver autoantibodies are negative, and a liver ultrasound shows no biliary dilatation or gallstones. Her fasting bile acid level today is 128 micromol/L, having been 46 micromol/L two weeks ago.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 84/min, blood pressure 112/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 °C, foetal heart rate 142/min
data_table.Investigations: Bile acids 128 micromol/L (<10), alanine aminotransferase 96 U/L (<35), bilirubin 12 micromol/L (<20), platelets 245 x10^9/L (150-400)
data_table.Imaging: Liver ultrasound shows no biliary dilatation and no gallstones, foetal growth on the 45th centile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate plan for timing of birth?

options.text: Plan birth at 35 to 36 weeks after a course of antenatal corticosteroids
options.rationale: Stillbirth risk rises steeply once bile acids exceed 100 micromol/L, and this threshold defines the group in whom earlier planned birth is justified. Corticosteroids are given because birth at this gestation carries neonatal respiratory risk. (Source: RANZCOG: Obstetric cholestasis)

options.text: Plan birth at 38 to 39 weeks with weekly bile acid monitoring until then
options.rationale: This timing suits women whose bile acids remain below 40 micromol/L, where the excess stillbirth risk is not clearly increased. It underestimates the risk carried by a level above 100 micromol/L. (Source: RANZCOG: Obstetric cholestasis)

options.text: Plan birth at 37 weeks with twice weekly cardiotocography until then
options.rationale: Cardiotocography does not predict the sudden stillbirth associated with this condition, so surveillance cannot substitute for earlier birth. The timing also does not reflect the severity band she now occupies. (Source: RANZCOG: Obstetric cholestasis)

options.text: Plan birth at 40 weeks and treat the itch with ursodeoxycholic acid until then
options.rationale: Ursodeoxycholic acid improves itch and biochemistry but has not been shown to reduce stillbirth, so it cannot justify expectant management to term. Treating the symptom does not address the risk. (Source: RANZCOG: Obstetric cholestasis)

options.text: Arrange birth within the next 24 hours by induction regardless of cervical status
options.rationale: Birth at 33 weeks would expose the baby to substantial prematurity risk that outweighs the stillbirth risk at this gestation. Immediate birth is reserved for other deteriorating features such as jaundice with coagulopathy. (Source: RANZCOG: Obstetric cholestasis)

explanation.summary: Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy is diagnosed by pruritus without a primary rash together with raised bile acids, after excluding other liver disease. Its significance is almost entirely foetal, and the pivotal insight from large cohort data is that risk is not uniform across the diagnosis but is concentrated in women with severe biochemical disease. Peak bile acid concentration stratifies that risk, with levels below 40 micromol/L carrying little excess stillbirth risk and levels of 100 micromol/L or above carrying a markedly elevated risk that justifies planned late preterm birth. Because the stillbirth is typically sudden rather than preceded by growth restriction or abnormal Dopplers, antenatal surveillance offers false reassurance and timing of birth is the only intervention shown to matter.
key_points: Diagnosis requires pruritus with raised bile acids and exclusion of other liver disease
Peak bile acid concentration stratifies stillbirth risk within the diagnosis
Levels of 100 micromol/L or above justify planned birth at 35 to 36 weeks
Cardiotocography and Doppler do not predict the sudden stillbirth
Ursodeoxycholic acid improves itch and biochemistry but not stillbirth risk
explanation.pearls: The 100 micromol/L bile acid threshold is the single number that changes management in cholestasis of pregnancy, moving planned birth from around 38 weeks to 35 to 36 weeks with corticosteroid cover.

subtopic_detail: Restarting clozapine for a man who stopped taking it for three days while unwell at home
stem:
A 38 year old man with treatment resistant schizophrenia attends your community mental health clinic. He has taken clozapine 400 mg at night for six years with good symptom control and no admissions in that time.

He had a bout of vomiting and diarrhoea over the weekend and did not take any clozapine on Saturday, Sunday or Monday. He restarted his usual night time dose last night of his own accord and now feels lightheaded on standing. He has no fever, no chest pain and no constipation, and his mental state is unchanged with no return of hallucinations. His full blood count today is normal and his observations show a postural drop in blood pressure.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 96/min, blood pressure 102/62 mmHg lying with a fall to 84/50 mmHg standing, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 6.8 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), neutrophils 4.1 x10^9/L (2.0-7.5), C-reactive protein within normal limits
data_table.Medication: Clozapine 400 mg nightly for six years, no doses taken Saturday to Monday, full dose resumed last night

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of his clozapine?

options.text: Continue the current dose and monitor his blood pressure closely over the next few days
options.rationale: Continuing at the full dose after tolerance has been lost is the exact scenario that has caused deaths from cardiovascular collapse and seizures. Monitoring does not mitigate a dose the patient can no longer tolerate. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Cease the current dose and retitrate from 12.5 mg daily using the standard escalation schedule
options.rationale: Tolerance to the cardiovascular effects of clozapine is lost after more than 48 hours without a dose, so resuming the previous dose risks severe hypotension, sedation and seizures. Retitration from the starting dose rebuilds tolerance safely, and it can usually be done faster than an initial titration. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Halve the current dose to 200 mg nightly and increase back to 400 mg over the next week
options.rationale: Any dose substantially above the starting dose carries the same tolerance related risk, and halving is an arbitrary compromise rather than a recognised approach. The safe restart point is the initial titration dose. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Cease clozapine permanently and commence olanzapine at an equivalent antipsychotic dose
options.rationale: Abandoning an agent that has given six years of remission in treatment resistant illness would very likely lead to relapse. A missed dose interval is a titration problem, not a reason to change drug. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Continue the current dose and add fludrocortisone to manage the postural blood pressure drop
options.rationale: Treating the symptom leaves the underlying dosing hazard in place and adds a drug with its own risks. The hypotension is a signal that the dose is no longer tolerated. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

explanation.summary: Clozapine is reserved for treatment resistant schizophrenia and carries a set of hazards that require structured monitoring, including neutropenia, myocarditis in the first weeks, constipation progressing to ileus, seizures and cardiometabolic effects. A less well known but clinically critical hazard is the rapid loss of tolerance to its cardiovascular and sedative effects during a break in treatment. When more than 48 hours of doses are missed, the patient must be retitrated from the starting dose rather than resuming their previous maintenance dose, because reinstating the full dose has caused profound hypotension, respiratory depression, seizures and death. Breaks in treatment are common during physical illness, hospital admission and disruption to supply, so the question of how many doses were missed should be asked routinely whenever a patient on clozapine presents.
key_points: Tolerance to clozapine's cardiovascular effects is lost after more than 48 hours
A break of more than two days requires retitration from the starting dose
Retitration after a break can usually proceed faster than initial titration
Physical illness and admission are common causes of unplanned breaks
Ask specifically how many doses were missed at every presentation
explanation.pearls: The 48 hour rule is the one clozapine number that changes management at the bedside: beyond that gap the maintenance dose becomes unsafe and titration restarts at 12.5 mg regardless of how long the patient has been stable.

subtopic_detail: Antibiotic choice for moderate community acquired pneumonia in a man with a documented anaphylactic reaction to penicillin
stem:
A 62 year old man presents to your emergency department with four days of fever, productive cough and right sided pleuritic chest pain. He is admitted under your medical team.

His medical record documents an episode ten years ago in which amoxicillin caused urticaria, lip swelling and hypotension requiring adrenaline in an emergency department. He has no other allergies. On examination he has bronchial breathing at the right base with dullness to percussion. His chest radiograph shows right lower lobe consolidation without effusion. His severity assessment places him in the moderate category requiring inpatient intravenous therapy.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 108/min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 26/min, SpO2 92% on room air, temperature 38.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Bronchial breathing and dullness to percussion at the right base, no signs of effusion
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 16.8 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), C-reactive protein 186 mg/L (<5), urea 7.2 mmol/L (3.0-8.0), chest radiograph shows right lower lobe consolidation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Intravenous ceftriaxone with oral doxycycline and review when culture results return
options.rationale: Cephalosporins retain a beta lactam ring and, although cross reactivity with later generation agents is lower than once believed, they are avoided after a documented anaphylactic reaction. The atypical cover is appropriate but the primary agent is not. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Intravenous benzylpenicillin with oral doxycycline and review when culture results return
options.rationale: This is the standard regimen for moderate community acquired pneumonia but is absolutely contraindicated by his documented anaphylaxis to a penicillin. Rechallenge risks a fatal reaction. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Intravenous vancomycin with oral azithromycin and review when culture results return
options.rationale: Vancomycin has no activity against the Gram negative and atypical organisms relevant here and does not cover the common causative pathogen adequately in this context. It is reserved for suspected resistant staphylococcal infection. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Intravenous moxifloxacin as a single agent with review when culture results return
options.rationale: A respiratory fluoroquinolone covers both typical and atypical pathogens and avoids the beta lactam ring entirely, which is necessary after a documented immediate hypersensitivity reaction. Monotherapy is adequate because its spectrum replaces both components of the standard combination. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Oral doxycycline as a single agent with review when culture results return and reassessment daily
options.rationale: Oral monotherapy with an agent lacking reliable pneumococcal activity is insufficient for pneumonia requiring inpatient intravenous treatment. Severity determines the route as well as the spectrum. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Community acquired pneumonia is treated according to severity, and Australian practice uses a severity tool to decide between oral outpatient therapy, intravenous inpatient therapy and intensive care level treatment with broadened cover. Standard moderate severity treatment combines a beta lactam for typical organisms with doxycycline or a macrolide for atypical organisms. A genuine immediate hypersensitivity reaction, characterised by urticaria, angioedema, bronchospasm or hypotension within an hour of a dose, excludes the whole beta lactam group including cephalosporins in the acute setting, and a respiratory fluoroquinolone becomes the appropriate substitute because it covers both halves of the usual regimen. Distinguishing this from a delayed non-severe rash matters greatly, since the majority of patients labelled penicillin allergic are not, and inaccurate labels lead to worse outcomes through use of broader and less effective agents. Formal allergy assessment and delabelling should be arranged after recovery.
key_points: Severity assessment determines route, spectrum and site of care
Standard moderate therapy pairs a beta lactam with atypical cover
Immediate hypersensitivity excludes the beta lactam group in the acute setting
A respiratory fluoroquinolone covers both typical and atypical organisms alone
Most patients labelled penicillin allergic are not, and delabelling improves outcomes
explanation.pearls: A documented reaction with hypotension and angioedema within an hour is an immediate hypersensitivity that rules out cephalosporins acutely, whereas an isolated delayed maculopapular rash does not and should prompt referral for delabelling rather than lifelong avoidance.

sources.label: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy: Penicillin allergy

subtopic_detail: Oral iron dose and duration for a toddler drinking large volumes of cow milk with microcytic anaemia
stem:
An 18 month old boy is brought to your clinic because he is pale and his parents feel he tires easily at playgroup. He drinks about a litre and a half of cow milk each day and eats very little solid food. He was born at term and his development is age appropriate.

His parents are both well and there is no family history of anaemia or blood disorders. His examination is unremarkable apart from pallor, with no organomegaly and no dysmorphic features. His blood film is reported as showing hypochromic microcytic red cells without target cells or basophilic stippling.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 118/min, blood pressure 92/54 mmHg, respiratory rate 26/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 °C
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 92 g/L (110-140), mean cell volume 64 fL (73-85), ferritin 7 micrograms/L (20-200), C-reactive protein within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Pallor of conjunctivae and palmar creases, no hepatosplenomegaly, no lymphadenopathy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment plan?

options.text: Elemental iron 3 mg/kg once daily ceased as soon as the haemoglobin has returned to normal
options.rationale: Stopping at haemoglobin normalisation leaves stores depleted and the anaemia predictably recurs. The haemoglobin recovers well before ferritin does. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron deficiency)

options.text: Dietary modification alone with reduced milk intake and review of the blood count in three months
options.rationale: Diet alone is too slow to correct an established deficiency of this degree, though it is essential to prevent recurrence. It would be appropriate for borderline iron status without anaemia. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron deficiency)

options.text: Intravenous iron infusion arranged as a day case with dietary advice given at the same visit
options.rationale: Parenteral iron is reserved for failed or not tolerated oral therapy, malabsorption, or ongoing losses, none of which has been established here. Oral therapy has not yet been tried. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook Children's Dosing Companion)
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook Children's Dosing Companion

options.text: Packed red cell transfusion followed by oral iron and outpatient haematology review
options.rationale: Transfusion is for haemodynamic compromise or symptomatic severe anaemia, and this child is stable with a haemoglobin well above that threshold. It would also delay the diagnostic value of the response to iron. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron deficiency)

options.text: Elemental iron 3 mg/kg once daily continued for three months after the haemoglobin normalises
options.rationale: Replacement corrects the haemoglobin within weeks but the stores take far longer, so treatment continues past normalisation to refill ferritin and prevent early relapse. Reducing milk volume and increasing iron rich solids is given alongside the supplement. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron deficiency)

explanation.summary: Iron deficiency is the commonest nutritional deficiency in Australian toddlers and excessive cow milk intake is the classic driver, displacing iron rich solids and causing occult gut blood loss. The diagnosis rests on a microcytic hypochromic picture with a low ferritin, remembering that ferritin is an acute phase reactant and can be falsely normal during inflammation. Treatment is oral elemental iron with a deliberate continuation phase after the haemoglobin corrects, because haemoglobin recovery precedes store repletion by months. Failure to respond should prompt review of adherence, of ongoing losses, and of alternative diagnoses such as thalassaemia trait.
key_points: Cow milk intake above about 500 mL daily in toddlers displaces dietary iron
Ferritin is an acute phase reactant and can be falsely normal with inflammation
Haemoglobin corrects within weeks but stores need months of continued therapy
A reticulocyte rise within a week supports the diagnosis
Persistent failure to respond prompts review for thalassaemia trait or blood loss
explanation.pearls: Continue oral iron for three months beyond haemoglobin normalisation: stopping the day the count is normal is the single commonest reason a toddler is back with the same microcytic anaemia six months later.

sources.label: Australian Medicines Handbook Children's Dosing Companion

subtopic_detail: Anti-D requirement for a woman with a rhesus negative blood group and light bleeding at ten weeks with a closed cervix
stem:
A 27 year old woman in her second pregnancy attends your early pregnancy assessment unit at 10 weeks with two days of light vaginal bleeding, described as spotting that does not fill a pad. She has mild period like cramping that settles with paracetamol.

Her first pregnancy ended in a normal vaginal birth three years ago and she received anti-D immunoglobulin after that birth. Speculum examination shows a closed cervical os with a small amount of old blood in the vagina, and no products are visible. Ultrasound today confirms a single intrauterine pregnancy with a foetal heart rate of 164/min and a crown rump length consistent with dates. Her blood group is confirmed as O negative and her antibody screen is negative.

data_table.Examination: Closed cervical os, small amount of old blood in the vagina, no products of conception visible, uterus non-tender
data_table.Investigations: Blood group O negative, antibody screen negative, haemoglobin 128 g/L (115-155)
data_table.Imaging: Single intrauterine pregnancy, foetal heart rate 164/min, crown rump length consistent with 10 weeks

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of her rhesus status?

options.text: Give 250 IU of anti-D immunoglobulin now and repeat the dose if bleeding continues
options.rationale: Giving anti-D for a threatened miscarriage at this gestation exposes her to a blood product without evidence of benefit. The 250 IU dose is correct for first trimester sensitising events, but this is not one. (Source: RANZCOG: Guidelines for the use of Rh D immunoglobulin)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Guidelines for the use of Rh D immunoglobulin

options.text: Withhold anti-D immunoglobulin and manage expectantly with review if bleeding worsens
options.rationale: Anti-D is not required for threatened miscarriage before 12 weeks where the pregnancy remains viable and there has been no instrumentation, because the foeto-maternal transfusion volume is negligible. Routine prophylaxis will still be given in the third trimester. (Source: RANZCOG: Guidelines for the use of Rh D immunoglobulin)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Guidelines for the use of Rh D immunoglobulin

options.text: Give 625 IU of anti-D immunoglobulin now and arrange a Kleihauer test the same day
options.rationale: The larger dose and quantification of foeto-maternal haemorrhage apply to sensitising events after 12 weeks, not to first trimester bleeding. Both the dose and the test are mismatched to the gestation. (Source: RANZCOG: Guidelines for the use of Rh D immunoglobulin)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Guidelines for the use of Rh D immunoglobulin

options.text: Arrange non-invasive foetal rhesus genotyping now and give anti-D only if the result is positive
options.rationale: Foetal genotyping from maternal blood is not part of routine Australian practice and would not alter management at this gestation. The decision here rests on whether a sensitising event has occurred. (Source: RANZCOG: Guidelines for the use of Rh D immunoglobulin)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Guidelines for the use of Rh D immunoglobulin

options.text: Withhold anti-D immunoglobulin now and omit the routine third trimester doses as well
options.rationale: Routine antenatal prophylaxis at 28 and 34 weeks is given to all rhesus negative women regardless of first trimester events. Omitting it would leave her unprotected against silent sensitisation. (Source: RANZCOG: Guidelines for the use of Rh D immunoglobulin)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Guidelines for the use of Rh D immunoglobulin

explanation.summary: Rhesus D alloimmunisation is prevented by giving anti-D immunoglobulin routinely in the third trimester, after birth of a rhesus positive baby, and after potentially sensitising events. The distinction that causes most difficulty in early pregnancy is between a threatened miscarriage with a viable pregnancy and a genuine sensitising event such as miscarriage with instrumentation, ectopic pregnancy, termination, or chorionic villus sampling. Before 12 weeks the foeto-maternal transfusion volume in uncomplicated threatened miscarriage is too small to sensitise, so anti-D is not indicated. Dose also varies by gestation, with 250 IU covering first trimester events and 625 IU used after 12 weeks alongside a Kleihauer test to detect a larger bleed requiring additional doses.
key_points: Threatened miscarriage before 12 weeks with a viable pregnancy does not need anti-D
Instrumentation, ectopic pregnancy and termination are sensitising at any gestation
First trimester sensitising events are covered by a 250 IU dose
After 12 weeks the dose is 625 IU with a Kleihauer test to quantify the bleed
Routine prophylaxis at 28 and 34 weeks is given irrespective of earlier events
explanation.pearls: Anti-D must be given within 72 hours of a sensitising event to be reliably effective, though it is still worth giving up to ten days later if the window has been missed.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Guidelines for the use of Rh D immunoglobulin
National Blood Authority Australia: Anti-D immunoglobulin

subtopic_detail: Timing of the first buprenorphine dose for a man who last used a long acting opioid the previous evening
stem:
A 34 year old man attends your addiction medicine clinic wanting to start opioid replacement treatment. He has been using illicitly obtained slow release oral morphine and last took a dose at 8 pm yesterday, about fourteen hours ago.

He is keen to take his first dose immediately and is frustrated at the suggestion of waiting. On examination he is mildly anxious and restless with a pulse rate of 92/min, but his pupils are mid-sized rather than dilated, he has no sweating, no gooseflesh, no lacrimation and no yawning. His objective withdrawal score is 5. He has no other medical conditions and takes no other sedating medication.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 92/min, blood pressure 128/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Mildly anxious and restless, mid-sized pupils, no sweating, gooseflesh, lacrimation or yawning
data_table.Assessment: Objective opioid withdrawal score 5, last slow release morphine dose fourteen hours ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate approach to his first dose?

options.text: Give the first dose now, since fourteen hours since his last use is a sufficient interval
options.rationale: The interval alone is not sufficient for a slow release preparation, whose duration of action extends well beyond that of immediate release opioids. The objective score rather than the clock determines readiness. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction Medicine)

options.text: Give the first dose now with an antiemetic and clonidine to cover any withdrawal symptoms
options.rationale: Symptomatic cover does not prevent precipitated withdrawal, which can be severe and prolonged and frequently causes patients to disengage from treatment. The timing problem is not solved pharmacologically. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction Medicine)

options.text: Wait until his objective withdrawal features score in the moderate range before the first dose
options.rationale: Buprenorphine has high receptor affinity with partial agonist activity, so giving it while substantial full agonist still occupies the receptor displaces that agonist and precipitates withdrawal. Waiting until objective withdrawal is established confirms the receptor is sufficiently free. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction Medicine)

options.text: Start methadone today instead and reconsider transferring him to buprenorphine in a month
options.rationale: Switching agent avoids the timing issue but commits him to a drug with a narrower safety margin during induction and greater overdose risk. His preference and circumstances have not been shown to favour it. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction Medicine)

options.text: Give naloxone first to clear the receptor and then start buprenorphine an hour afterwards
options.rationale: Naloxone would itself precipitate severe withdrawal and has no role in planned induction. It is used for opioid overdose with respiratory depression. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction Medicine)

explanation.summary: Buprenorphine is a high affinity partial agonist at the mu opioid receptor, and this pharmacology explains both its safety advantages and its main induction hazard. Because it binds more avidly than most full agonists, giving it while the receptor remains substantially occupied displaces the full agonist and replaces a high level of activation with a lower one, producing abrupt and severe precipitated withdrawal. Induction is therefore timed by objective withdrawal features rather than by the interval since last use, using a structured scale, and the required wait is longer after long acting preparations such as slow release morphine or methadone than after short acting opioids. Subjective distress alone is not adequate evidence of readiness, since anxiety and drug seeking can be present well before the receptor is free. Once established, buprenorphine carries a lower overdose risk than methadone because of its ceiling effect on respiratory depression.
key_points: Buprenorphine displaces full agonists because of its higher receptor affinity
Induction is timed by objective withdrawal features, not hours since last use
Long acting opioids require a longer wait than short acting ones
Subjective distress alone does not confirm readiness for the first dose
The ceiling effect on respiratory depression makes maintenance safer than methadone
explanation.pearls: Precipitated withdrawal from a too early buprenorphine dose can last many hours and is the single commonest reason a patient refuses to attempt opioid replacement again, so the wait for objective signs is a retention issue as much as a comfort one.

subtopic_detail: Management of an international normalised ratio of six point five on warfarin with no bleeding before elective surgery
stem:
A 74 year old woman taking warfarin for atrial fibrillation attends your anticoagulation clinic for a routine check three weeks before an elective hip replacement. Her target range is 2.0 to 3.0 and her results have been stable for months.

She completed a course of trimethoprim with sulfamethoxazole for a urinary infection last week. She reports no bruising, no bleeding from the gums or nose, no blood in the urine or stool and no headache. Her examination reveals no bruising or other signs of bleeding. Her international normalised ratio today is 6.5 and her haemoglobin is unchanged from her last check.

data_table.Examination: No bruising, petechiae or other signs of bleeding, no abdominal tenderness, no neurological signs
data_table.Investigations: International normalised ratio 6.5 (target 2.0-3.0), haemoglobin 128 g/L (115-155), platelets 232 x10^9/L (150-400), creatinine within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Withhold warfarin alone and repeat the measurement in two days without giving vitamin K
options.rationale: Omitting doses alone is the correct approach for modest elevation below about 4.5, but at this level the correction is too slow. The bleeding risk during the delay is what makes it inadequate. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Withhold warfarin and give low dose oral vitamin K, with a repeat measurement the next day
options.rationale: At this degree of over-anticoagulation without bleeding, withholding doses alone corrects too slowly and leaves a period of substantial bleeding risk, so a small oral dose of vitamin K is added. Low dose oral therapy avoids the prolonged warfarin resistance that follows larger parenteral doses. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Withhold warfarin and give intravenous vitamin K 10 mg, with a repeat measurement the next day
options.rationale: A large parenteral dose over-corrects and produces warfarin resistance lasting up to a week, which is a particular problem before planned surgery requiring bridging. The high dose is reserved for major bleeding. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Withhold warfarin and give prothrombin complex concentrate, with a repeat measurement the next day
options.rationale: Factor concentrate is reserved for major or life threatening bleeding, or for urgent surgery that cannot wait, and carries thrombotic risk. She is not bleeding and her surgery is three weeks away. (Source: National Blood Authority Australia: Patient blood management)
source_refs: National Blood Authority Australia: Patient blood management

options.text: Continue warfarin at a reduced dose and repeat the measurement in one week without other action
options.rationale: Continuing any warfarin while the level is this high prolongs the period of excess anticoagulation. Dose adjustment addresses future stability rather than the present risk. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

explanation.summary: Management of an elevated international normalised ratio on warfarin is determined by two variables: whether the patient is bleeding, and how high the value is. In the absence of bleeding, values up to about 4.5 are managed by withholding doses and rechecking, values between roughly 4.5 and 10 warrant withholding plus a low oral dose of vitamin K, and values above 10 warrant a somewhat larger oral dose. Any significant bleeding changes the approach entirely, requiring intravenous vitamin K together with prothrombin complex concentrate for major or life threatening haemorrhage. The reason low dose oral vitamin K is preferred when there is no bleeding is that larger parenteral doses cause over-correction and resistance to re-anticoagulation for several days, which matters for a patient who needs to return to therapeutic range. Identifying the precipitant is equally important, and antibiotics, particularly trimethoprim with sulfamethoxazole and metronidazole, are among the commonest causes through inhibition of warfarin metabolism.
key_points: Management depends on the presence of bleeding and on the height of the value
Withholding alone suffices below about 4.5 without bleeding
Low dose oral vitamin K is added between roughly 4.5 and 10
Large parenteral doses cause resistance to re-anticoagulation for days
Antibiotics are among the commonest precipitants through metabolic inhibition
explanation.pearls: Trimethoprim with sulfamethoxazole is one of the most potent potentiators of warfarin, and an international normalised ratio check within three to five days of starting it prevents exactly this presentation.

sources.label: National Blood Authority Australia: Patient blood management

subtopic_detail: Alarm versus desmopressin choice for a nine year old with bedwetting only and a normal daytime pattern
stem:
A 9 year old boy is brought to your practice because he still wets the bed most nights, which is now stopping him accepting invitations to sleep at friends' houses. He has never had a sustained period of dry nights.

He passes urine four to five times during the day with no urgency, no daytime wetting and no pain. He opens his bowels daily without straining. His examination including abdominal, genital, spinal and lower limb neurological assessment is normal, and his urine dipstick and blood glucose are normal. His parents are motivated and ask what will give him the best chance of lasting dryness, mentioning that a school camp is scheduled in eight months.

data_table.Examination: Normal abdominal, genital and spinal examination, normal lower limb tone power and reflexes
data_table.Investigations: Urine dipstick negative for glucose protein blood and leucocytes, random blood glucose 4.8 mmol/L (3.5-7.8)

lead_in: What treatment would you recommend first?

options.text: Enuresis alarm used consistently every night, with review of progress at four weeks
options.rationale: The alarm produces the highest rate of sustained dryness after treatment stops, which matches this family's stated goal and their capacity to persist. The timeframe before camp comfortably allows a full alarm course. (Source: RCH CPG: Enuresis)

options.text: Oral desmopressin taken each night, with review of progress at four weeks
options.rationale: Desmopressin suppresses wetting while it is being taken but relapse on stopping is common, so it suits short term cover such as a single camp rather than a durable cure. Here there is ample time for definitive treatment. (Source: RCH CPG: Enuresis)

options.text: Fluid restriction after the evening meal with a scheduled lift to the toilet overnight
options.rationale: Lifting a sleeping child does not teach the arousal response and simply empties the bladder, and severe evening fluid restriction is not effective as sole therapy. These measures support but do not replace definitive treatment. (Source: RCH CPG: Enuresis)

options.text: Oral oxybutynin at night with a bladder diary kept over the following four weeks
options.rationale: Anticholinergic therapy targets detrusor overactivity, which typically shows as daytime urgency and frequency, and this boy has an entirely normal daytime pattern. It would be considered where alarm and desmopressin have both failed. (Source: RCH CPG: Enuresis)

options.text: Referral for renal tract ultrasound and urodynamic studies before any treatment is started
options.rationale: Imaging and urodynamics are reserved for daytime symptoms, abnormal examination, or treatment resistant cases, none of which applies to uncomplicated monosymptomatic bedwetting. His assessment is entirely normal. (Source: RCH CPG: Enuresis)

explanation.summary: Monosymptomatic nocturnal enuresis means bedwetting with a normal daytime voiding pattern and no other urinary symptoms, and it is distinguished from non-monosymptomatic enuresis because the two are managed differently. Constipation must be excluded and treated first because it is a common reversible contributor. The alarm and desmopressin both work but differ in what they achieve: the alarm conditions arousal and gives the best chance of dryness that persists after treatment ends, while desmopressin acts only while it is taken and is best used for short term cover of specific events. Choosing between them therefore depends on whether the family wants a durable cure or immediate cover, and on their capacity to persist with a device that wakes the household.
key_points: Monosymptomatic enuresis requires a normal daytime voiding pattern
Treat coexisting constipation before starting enuresis specific therapy
The alarm gives the highest sustained dryness after treatment stops
Desmopressin suits short term cover such as camps and sleepovers
Imaging is reserved for daytime symptoms or abnormal examination
explanation.pearls: Alarm training needs a minimum of six to eight weeks of consistent nightly use before it is judged to have failed, so it is the wrong choice when a family needs dryness for an event only days away.
